verdicts.summary: A stalled fetch now holds one of 4 shared permits for up to ~5 min. While 4 are stalled, every other repo's status fetch stays queued, and its waiter returns silently with success after 5s.
verdicts.scenario:
1. Four repos with hung remotes each start a status fetch. Each takes a permit from `statusFetchProcesses` (line 925) and runs up to 5 min.
2. A fifth repo's status poll forks its fetch at line 697. The fiber blocks in `withPermits(1)` at line 691.
3. The waiter times out at 5s (line 704) and logs only at debug level. `refreshStatusRemoteCacheEntry` returns `true`, so the Cache holds a success for 15s.
4. No failure is recorded, so `retryAt` and the cooldown never apply. Later polls join the same queued fiber.
5. The fifth repo's refs stay stale until a permit frees, up to ~5 min. Before this commit each fetch ran inline with its own 5s timeout and no shared cap.
verdicts.consequence: Ahead/behind counts for healthy repos stay stale for up to ~5 min. There is no warning log or backoff entry, so the stall is hard to diagnose. The shared 4-permit cap is new in this commit.
verdicts.missing: Per-remote isolation, or a log or failure record when a fetch is queued rather than running.

verdicts.summary: The unbounded `Fiber.await(pending)` before the pull is exactly finding 0. The rest of the note holds: the retry only fires for a lock failure with HEAD and branch unchanged.
`forceKillAfterMs` reaches the spawner as `forceKillAfter`. When it is unset the spawner behaves as before. When set, a plain number is read as milliseconds.
verdicts.scenario: Every other `execute` caller leaves it unset, so `ChildProcess.make` gets `forceKillAfter: undefined`. Line 484 uses `Predicate.isUndefined`, so that case keeps the old 1s wait with no SIGKILL. The option type is `Duration.Input` (ChildProcess.ts:269), which includes a number, so 1_000 is 1s and the SIGKILL branch at lines 487-490 applies. The scope finalizers at lines 550-559 pass `cmd.options`, so the timeout interruption in `executeRaw` also uses it.

verdicts.summary: The pull awaits a pending status fetch only once, before its first attempt. The ref-lock fallback retry never re-checks `statusFetches`, so a status fetch started during the pull can make the retry fail on the same ref.
verdicts.scenario:
1. No status fetch is pending at line 2667, so the pull does not wait.
2. During the pull (up to 30s), a 15s status poll runs `refreshStatusUpstreamIfStale`. `fetchRemoteForStatus` has no knowledge of the pull, so it forks a fetch for the same remote.
3. The pull's fetch and the status fetch update `refs/remotes/<remote>/<branch>` at about the same time. The pull hits a lock failure on that ref.
4. At line 2693 the fallback runs `pull --ff-only -- remote mergeRef`. It does not re-read `statusFetches` or await the fiber.
5. If the status fetch still holds the upstream ref lock, the retry fails on the same ref. The user gets 'Git could not update a local reference…'. I did not read any lock that stops status polls during a pull.
verdicts.consequence: A pull can fail with a transient ref-lock error that waiting for the in-flight status fetch would have avoided. The lock window is short, so this is rare.
verdicts.missing: Re-check `statusFetches` and await the pending fetch before the fallback retry.
